newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada takes strong measures to save pensions.
newsitem.headline: Canada takes strong measures to save pensions.

text.p: Canada's government proposed a whopping tax increase on Friday to ensure the viability of its social security fund when baby boomers retire.

In a move likely to be watched by the United States, it also proposed that the fund be allowed to invest in stocks and bonds like any other pension plan, possibly signaling a huge flow of funds into those markets.
"It is my privilege to table draft legislation that secures the future of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP)," Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said in Parliament.
The proposal is almost certain to become law since the ruling Liberals have a solid parliamentary majority.

Martin said that CPP rates would rise in the next six years by almost 70 percent to a combined 9.9 percent of insurable earnings from the current 5.85 percent. Employers and employees would split this equally.
The pension plan rates would still be less than in the United States, although overall income taxes are generally much higher in Canada.

Martin said that without the increase in premiums, the fund would have gone bankrupt in less than 20 years as baby boomers began to collect their pensions. He said the government would have eventually needed to raise premiums to more than 14 percent.
"This is not fair. This is not affordable," Martin said.
Martin's proposal was innovative in proposing to lift investment restrictions on the fund's reserves.

Currently, the CPP invests only in non-negotiable provincial bonds and at the preferred rate that would apply to the federal government, rather than the higher rates that provinces usually have to pay.
The draft legislation would allow it to invest in a diversified portfolio of securities just like private pension plans.

Midland Walwyn Chief Economist Mark Mullins said the fund's reserves should eventually reach C$100 billion ($75 billion) from the current C$40 billion ($30 billion), much of it funnelled into private stocks and bonds.
But he said that the effect of the tax increase was not going to stimulate the economy.
"People are falling off their chairs over here (over the size of the increase)," he said.

In January, a federal advisory panel in the United States recommended investing some of the U.S. Social Security trust funds in the stock market. Currently they can only be invested in treasury securities, which provide a lower rate of return than the private market.

"Canada's retirement income system is not alone in facing challenges from an aging population and increasing longevity," Martin said. "But almost no other industrialized country has done as much as Canada has to come to grips with these problems."
